title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM THE UNFINISHED TOWER
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM THE UNFINISHED TOWER
The tower stood there like a wound.

Concrete pillars reached toward the sky and then stopped as if someone had simply walked away from the dream that once lived there. Rust stained the exposed steel. Rain had carved dark trails down the unfinished walls. Grass pushed through cracks where workers once stood.
But one day I could not stop looking.
Because suddenly I realized that tower looked a lot like me.
Maybe it looks a little like you too.
There are few things more painful than beginning with passion and ending with abandonment.
The dream remains standing, but unfinished.
The vision remains visible, but incomplete.
The structure remains, but the builder is gone.
And eventually we begin to believe that the unfinished parts of our lives are evidence that God has given up on us.
But Scripture tells a different story.
When Jesus spoke about unfinished towers, He was not merely discussing construction projects.
"For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?"
The Greek word translated "complete" is τελέσαι (telesai), derived from τέλος (telos), meaning completion, fulfillment, intended purpose, or finished end.
This is the same family of words Jesus used on the cross when He cried:
The unfinished tower teaches us something profound about the human condition.
Human beings are experts at starting.
God is the Master of completion.
That truth becomes even more beautiful when we realize how often Scripture presents people as unfinished projects.
Yet none of their stories ended where their failures occurred.
Because God writes differently than we do.
The Hebrew language gives us a beautiful glimpse into this truth.
The word for grace is חֵן (chen).
It carries the idea of favor, kindness, beauty, and undeserved acceptance.
When grace enters a story, it rewrites expectations.
That is why the Gospel remains the most powerful story ever told.
Not because it hides human scandal.
The Bible never attempts to airbrush its heroes.
And then Jesus enters the story.
There may be someone reading this who feels like an unfinished tower.
You remember the version of yourself that loved God more deeply.
You remember prayers that felt alive.
You remember faith that felt stronger.
You remember dreams that seemed possible.
Now all you see are exposed beams and unfinished walls.
You wonder if He is disappointed every time He looks at you.
But Scripture reveals a God whose specialty is rebuilding.
The prophet Joel records God's promise:
"I will restore to you the years that the locust has eaten."
The Hebrew word is שָׁלַם (shalam), carrying the idea of restoring, repaying, making whole again.
God is not merely interested in repairing damage.
He restores what appeared permanently lost.
That is why the cross changes everything.
The cross was humanity's greatest scandal.
The innocent Son of God publicly executed.
Yet through grace it became the greatest victory in history.
Only God can transform a scandal into salvation.
Only God can transform an execution into redemption.
Only God can transform a sinner into a saint.
Only God can transform an unfinished tower into a testimony.
Perhaps that is why the Apostle Paul wrote with such confidence:
"He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion."
The Greek phrase ἐπιτελέσει (epitelesei) means to carry through fully, accomplish completely, finish perfectly.
The Gospel has never been the story of strong people impressing God.
It has always been the story of a perfect Savior rescuing weak people.
The unfinished tower is not proof that God abandoned the project.
It may simply be evidence that construction is still underway.
But no one judges a masterpiece while the Builder is still working.
The enemy wants you to believe your unfinished places define you.
The enemy points to your scandal.
The enemy points to your failures.
Jesus points to His finished work.
The enemy points to what broke.
Jesus points to what He is rebuilding.
And maybe that is the lesson hidden inside every unfinished tower.
Not all unfinished things are failures.
Some are simply waiting for the Builder to continue His work.
So before you condemn yourself, remember this:
The same Christ who cried Tetelestai over the work of redemption is still completing the work He started in His people.
And grace is still writing chapters you cannot yet see.
If this article stirred something deep in your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
What unfinished area of your life are you trusting Jesus to rebuild?
Someone else may find courage through your testimony.
And if you know someone who feels like their life has become an unfinished tower, share this with them today.
Because one day, when all the scaffolding comes down, you will discover that what looked unfinished was actually grace under construction.
